name: Shield graft (nasal tip)

card.summary: A rhinoplasty cartilage graft shaped like a shield and placed on the nasal tip to add definition and projection.
card.note: Surgical procedure; outcomes depend on surgeon and cartilage source.

quick.overview:
A shield graft is a piece of cartilage, usually shaped like a shield, sewn onto the front of the nasal tip during rhinoplasty. It makes the tip more defined and can push it further out from the face.
People seek it for a more refined, projected tip, which can improve nose-to-face balance.
quick.how: Surgeons harvest cartilage, commonly from the septum, and in revision cases from the ear or rib, and fix it to the tip, often through an open approach.
quick.risks: Rhinoplasty risks include tip deformities, asymmetry and the need for revision; surgery involves anesthesia and recovery.

lead: A shield graft is a piece of cartilage, cut roughly in the outline of a shield, that a surgeon sews onto the front of the nasal tip during rhinoplasty. It gives a rounded or blunt tip a more defined, sculpted look and can push the tip further forward, so the nose reads as more refined and better balanced against the rest of the face.[3][4]

Tip grafts exist for cases where sutures alone cannot change the shape of the lower lateral cartilages enough. A review of common nasal tip grafts concludes that cartilage grafts are a versatile option in that situation.[3] The shield graft is one of several named options, alongside onlay, columellar strut and septal extension grafts.[3][6]

Cartilage normally comes from the nasal septum; when the septum is insufficient, as in many revision operations, surgeons use ear (conchal) or rib cartilage.[4][5] Online, tip projection is discussed through measurements such as the Goode method, which aims for a tip distance of roughly 55 to 60 percent of the nasion-to-tip distance.[2][4]

chain: Cartilage shield sewn onto the tip
More definition and forward projection of the tip
More refined nose in profile and front view
angle.text: The graft reshapes the nasal tip, adding definition and forward projection. People use it to make a broad, under-projected or poorly defined tip look more refined and in better proportion with the face.

paras: The nasal tip is supported mainly by the paired lower lateral cartilages. Surgeons describe tip surgery as altering projection (how far the tip stands from the face), rotation (its upward or downward tilt) and definition or refinement of the tip lobule. A review of nasal tip surgery notes that tip maneuvers intended to change projection, rotation and refinement are central to rhinoplasty technique.[3]

A shield graft is placed on the front of the tip, in front of the domes, and is shaped so that its broad lower edge gives a defined tip and its position adds forward projection. It is often combined with other grafts. A 2025 retrospective study of 41 patients described a shield graft carved from rib cartilage paired with an onlay graft as a last step in refining the tip; three-dimensional measurements showed increases in tip projection, nasal length and Goode ratio, and the authors described it as a useful addition to the surgeon's toolkit.[5]

A related 2025 report described a 'shield-like' septal extension graft used in revision rhinoplasty, in a series of 18 patients followed for about a year, with no major complications and satisfactory aesthetic and functional results according to the authors; costal cartilage supplied the strength.[5]

Grafts for the tip are usually placed through an open approach, which uses a small incision across the columella plus incisions inside the nostrils. Wikipedia notes that the open approach gives better visualization, greater precision for tip work and easier graft harvesting, and that it is usually preferred in revision cases; the closed approach is associated with less swelling, less visible scarring and faster recovery. Systematic reviews report no significant long-term difference between the two in patient-reported outcomes, with the choice depending on surgeon expertise and anatomy.[4] The open approach itself dates to Aurel Rethi's work in 1934.[4]

Septal cartilage is the preferred donor material. When it is insufficient, ear (conchal) or rib (costal) cartilage is used, and donated rib cartilage and synthetic implants are further options.[4] Surgeons treating Asian noses, which are often described as having thick skin and weaker cartilage, have published many variants that use ear or rib cartilage for tip framework; a 2024 systematic review of nasal tip surgery in Asians identified lengthening the nose, projecting the tip and strengthening the tip framework as key goals.[5]

The Goode method draws a line perpendicular to the Frankfort plane through the alar-facial crease and compares the distance from that line to the tip with the nasion-to-tip distance. Wikipedia gives an ideal ratio of about 0.55 to 0.60.[4] A widely read looksmax.org thread explains the method and discusses how tip projection relates to jaw position: its author argues that a recessed jaw can make a nose look overprojected, and that overprojection can also occur with a well-positioned maxilla.[2]

Evidence on the shield graft specifically comes from surgical case series and comparisons rather than controlled trials. A 2026 study of 510 open rhinoplasty patients compared seven tip-support grafts and reported significant improvement in questionnaire scores in every graft group, with the shield, tongue-in-groove and tip-onlay groups scoring somewhat higher; the authors concluded that satisfaction cannot be credited to graft choice alone and stressed preoperative counseling.[6]

A review of ethnic rhinoplasty describes a structural approach that removes little tissue, reinforces support with sutures and grafts, and progresses gradually from simpler to more complex tip techniques, aiming for a more defined nose that harmonizes with the face.[1]

Rhinoplasty carries the general risks of surgery and anesthesia, and swelling can take a year or more to resolve fully; smoking impairs healing because of the nasal blood supply.[4] Revision surgery is reported in about 5 to 20 percent of rhinoplasties, for reasons such as breathing problems, asymmetry, a pinched tip or collapse.[4] Tip-related deformities named in the rhinoplasty literature include pollybeak, saddle nose and inverted-V, and excessive reduction of tip support is a recognised risk.[4] Harvesting rib or ear cartilage adds a donor site; a series of 39 patients with conchal grafts reported no donor-site morbidity.[6]

No randomized trial has been published on shield grafts alone. The available literature consists of reviews of nasal tip grafts,[3] case series of combined shield and onlay grafts,[5] and a 510-patient comparison of seven tip-support grafts that found improved patient-reported scores across groups.[6]

timeline.event: Aurel Rethi introduces the open approach to rhinoplasty, later the usual route for tip grafting.[4]
Padovan advocates open rhinoplasty; Wilfred Goodman later popularizes it.[4]
Gunter reports on open secondary rhinoplasty.[4]
A review in the Journal of Craniofacial Surgery surveys common nasal tip grafts.[3]
A systematic review examines nasal tip surgery techniques in Asian patients.[5]
A retrospective study reports combined shield and onlay rib-cartilage tip grafts in 41 patients.[5]
A study of 510 open rhinoplasty patients compares seven tip-support grafts.[6]

lore.intro: Tip projection and tip refinement are discussed on looksmax.org mainly in connection with the Goode method, jaw position and surgical options.[2]

claims.claim: Tip projection should be judged against the jaw and midface, not in isolation
claims.believers: Posters argue that a recessed maxilla or jaw can make a normal nose look overprojected, so jaw surgery may change how the nose reads.[2]
claims.experts: Rhinoplasty references describe the Goode ratio as a standard projection measure; surgeons plan tip work around overall facial proportions.[4]

claims.claim: A shield graft gives a more defined, projected tip
claims.believers: Surgeons who use tip grafts say grafts can change tip shape when sutures alone cannot adequately do so.[3]
claims.experts: A 2025 case series reported increased projection and Goode ratio after combined shield and onlay grafts,[5] and a 2026 comparison found improved questionnaire scores for shield grafts.[6]

claims.claim: Rib or ear cartilage can supply the graft when the septum cannot
claims.believers: Surgeons describe septal cartilage as the first choice and turn to ear or rib cartilage when the septum is insufficient, as in many revisions.[4]
claims.experts: Wikipedia and published series describe ear and rib cartilage as established alternative donor sites.[4][5]

claims.claim: Graft choice alone explains satisfaction with a result
claims.believers: Online discussion of tip surgery tends to focus on named techniques and measurements such as the Goode ratio.[2]
claims.experts: The 2026 comparison of seven grafts concluded that satisfaction cannot be attributed to graft choice alone.[6]
